data.buildstamp#buildstamp:
Read the Go build information of any binary, WebAssembly included, and fail one built from a modified tree. Repository → Latest tag: v0.2.0 (git ls-remote --tags, 2026-11-15); this page is written from the facts of v0.1.0, and the two are stated separately on purpose: which tag is current and which tag this page describes are different facts.
go version -m and debug/buildinfo answer “unrecognized file format” on a .wasm file. The go command writes the module information into every binary it links, between two 16-byte sentinels (infoStart and infoEnd in cmd/go/internal/modload/build.go). buildstamp finds them and parses the text with runtime/debug.ParseBuildInfo, so the same answer comes out of an ELF, a Mach-O, a PE or a WebAssembly module.
data.check#buildstamp check:
buildstamp check [--revision SHA] FILE... A file is clean when its build was stamped from an unmodified tree (vcs.modified is false) and, with --revision, from that commit. Every file is reported, even after the first failure.
Exit status: 0 every file is clean, 1 at least one is not (modified tree, no vcs stamp, or another revision), 2 a file is unreadable or carries no Go build information.
In a workflow, build outside the checkout and check against the commit under test:
go run github.com/go-fleettools/buildstamp/cmd/buildstamp@v0.1.0 \ check --revision "$GITHUB_SHA" "$RUNNER_TEMP/site/app.wasm"
data.package#Package: github.com/go-fleettools/buildstamp exposes ReadFile, Read, Setting and Clean(bi, wantRevision) for programs that need the same answer.
data.safety#Safety: Reads are bounded: 1 MiB of module information, and 1 GiB per file, checked by Stat before reading. FuzzRead runs in CI and the package is covered at 100% of statements. The tests build real js/wasm binaries, clean and dirty, and a CI lane runs the tool on its own build and on a planted dirty build that must exit 1.
data.show#buildstamp show: buildstamp show FILE... Prints the build information of each file: toolchain, module path and version, and the build settings.
data.why#Why: A CI build made after something wrote into the checkout is stamped vcs.modified=true and version v0.0.0-…+dirty. go-wasmcontainers/dashboard v0.4.2 shipped that way: its Pages job wrote _site/ inside the work tree before building.

data.dotgithub#.github:
Shared community health files, Renovate runner and preset for the go-fleettools organisation. Repository →
It has no tag, and no release: it is configuration, and its README is two lines long (a title and the sentence above). GitHub applies the community health files of a .github repository to the organisation’s repositories that have none of their own. There is nothing to install.

data.index#Files and functions, not only doma:
A repository’s name and description name its domain, never its functions, so fleetfind quantile used to print nothing in 2253 repositories while go-statistics/stats has quantile.go. The index adds file names and the exported top-level identifiers of every Go module, read from the Go module proxy (0 GitHub calls, incremental on pushed_at, bounded and zip-slip safe):
go-statistics/stats file:quantile.go go-statistics/stats ident:Quantile Every run says how many repositories were indexed, how many are not in the proxy (not a module, private, or unpublished: a blind spot, not a NO), and how many are UNREAD with the reason. A zero is never printed as nothing in N repositories when part of N could not be read.
data.ranking#Ranking:
A name beats a description: a path match scores 10 and a description or topic match 3. Every term must match, so two words narrow, they do not widen.
A hit is a lead, not an authority. Confirm it:
gh api repos// --jq '{full_name, id, pushed_at, archived}'
data.rules#What it will not let you believe: Every answer carries the date the inventory was taken, and one older than a day says so on stderr before it answers: a “nothing matches” is only as good as when it was measured. Zero results are said out loud, because a sweep that prints nothing is indistinguishable from one that could not read. An empty fleet is refused, twice and separately (no organisations listed; organisations that listed and brought back no repository), and neither writes an empty inventory over a good one. Archived repositories are found but not returned by default; -all asks for them, because knowing something moved is the useful answer.

data.built-in#What is built into them:
They say when they are not the code in this repository. A binary installed from an old tag is compared with what has changed for that command since. Every one answers -h with 0. redscan -h once ran a full sweep of every organisation and had to be killed; a test now fails any command that cannot answer -h. A sweep asks for the hourly API budget before spending it and refuses to begin below a floor, because that budget is per user and shared with the fleet’s Renovate runners. Four sweeps have emptied it and made those runs fail. A failed call must never become a verdict, and a deliberate budget stop is reported separately from “could not be read”: an unread repository is asked again, a budget stop is waited out. The secondary rate limit is not visible to rate_limit — measured 2026-10-10, gh answered 403 on every call while the budget read 5000/5000. ⛔ And two of them were blind to this fleet’s own pages until v0.67.0, which is the same failure one level up: a tool that is right about its rules and cannot read the subject answers confidently anyway.
tagcells keeps the version a page states equal to each module’s latest release. It looked for [[params.modules]] with tag = "vX.Y.Z"; the go-* landings are [[params.repos]] with label =. Against go-fleettools.github.io/hugo.toml it answered 0 cell(s) and exited 2 — rightly refusing to call nothing a pass, and the reason thirteen labels dated in a comment above them had never been checked. When it first could look, three of the thirteen were stale and fleettools' own was twenty-seven releases behind. pagetext reported text missing on a page that carried it, six retries running, because of an apostrophe: Hugo prints fleet’s where the source said fleet's, and the match decoded entities but not typographic punctuation. Every English possessive and contraction was a false negative. A verification tool that says “not published yet” about something published is worse than none — the next person reads a real failure the same way.

viaonly (v0.126.0, 2026-11-15) answers two questions about a package: which calls bypass the wrapper they were supposed to go through (--wraps/--via), and which exit points never ask the question the function exists to ask (--asks/--in). The second rule needed a second shape rather than a flag, because an early return does not read as an exit and a return is not a call. It credits only what is certainly evaluated: of A && B only A is, a case list is evaluated in order so only its first expression is, a clause reached by fallthrough evaluated none of its own, and a defer, a go statement or a function literal is never credited. ⛔ Its own first version let through exactly the defect it was written for: it credited “this statement contains a question”, so a question asked inside one switch case marked every later exit as having asked it — the defect’s second round, with the suite green and coverage full. What caught it was recalculating a twenty-row expectation table by hand, where five of the twenty were wrong; three further review rounds found ten real defects in it, each time against a green suite.
ratewait (v0.128.0, 2026-11-16) blocks until a named GitHub budget is at or above a threshold, and exists because nothing in the fleet could wait. The hourly budget is per user with about twenty-five sessions drawing on it, so a program meets a 403 it did nothing to cause, and fleet.Throttled answers false for API rate limit exceeded on purpose — that budget will not refill inside any backoff — which correctly ends the retry and leaves nobody able to come back at the reset. It sleeps to the reset the API reports rather than on an interval, because a poll loop spends the budget it is waiting for. ⛔ Four rounds of review each found its loop unbounded in a new way, and the result is a rule about waiting rather than about one command: a predicate over a value the remote reports is not a bound you control. Strictly later than the last reset, later by at least the margin and strictly in the future were each defeated by a reset that moves with the clock — the last measured at five readings in twelve seconds, about 1300 under a 65-minute deadline. What bounds it is a count of readings derived from the window the API’s own body shows (the farthest reset among fifteen resources is 59m59s), three plus one per hour the deadline allows; flooring that division refused a legitimate wait at --timeout 59m, and its own test had pinned the undercount as the specification, so a mutation raising the count was reported caught by an expectation that had moved with the defect. A + unit - 1 ceil also overflows int64 at the largest duration the flag parser accepts, which turned the longest wait askable into an instant refusal.
dashfix (v0.148.1, 2026-11-20) fixes one line of an organisation’s Renovate runner config on the branch of a red Renovate pull request, then waits for CI and merges it: dependencyDashboard: true becomes dependencyDashboard: { enabled: true }. Upstream Renovate migrated that key to an object, and the validator these repositories run (renovate@latest --strict) now exits 1 on the boolean, so every Renovate pull request in them was red for a reason its own diff does not show (#305). Targets are spelled owner/repo#number and handled one at a time. For each, the REST budget must hold --reserve requests (default 1000) and the trailing hour fewer than --max merged pull requests (default 20), or the run stops; the pull request must be open with a failed check (green or pending ones are skipped, never touched); agentsync claim must succeed (a repository somebody else holds is skipped and listed); a repository whose workflows carry RENOVATE_VERSION is skipped and listed, because aligning that pin is a different change. It then commits, pushes with gitpush, waits with prwait and merges with ghmerge only when prwait says green. Any command that fails or refuses stops the whole run with status 1 and is never retried another way; a skip is not a failure. --dry-run judges and edits nothing. Exit status: 0 every target merged or skipped, 1 something was refused, 2 the run could not start or stopped at a limit.
flakescan (merged 2026-11-19 in #367, released in v0.141.0) counts how often a named test has failed across a repository’s CI history, by lane, with a denominator. It exists because go-crdt/collab#204, one flake, had its sweep done by hand three times over three populations — commits on main, red runs on main, the pull request somebody happened to be on — and got three answers. ⛔ It reads runs × attempts, not runs. Run 39069166645 of that repository is attempt 2, conclusion success on a pull request, and its first attempt holds a failure of the test: a flake is precisely the failure that gets re-run, and a re-run repaints the run green while the evidence stays in attempt n−1, so a census over runs whose conclusion is failure cannot see what it counts and “N in M runs” is a floor. It also reads a failed step inside a green job (continue-on-error leaves the job green), every page of a job list (a short read is an error rather than a smaller answer), and only the logs of jobs that failed. Zero occurrences with anything unread exits 2, never 0, because GitHub discards logs on a retention window. First run, over the whole window of that issue — 257 runs, 265 attempts, 6296 jobs, 66 logs: 3 occurrences across two lanes (arch amd64 2, test (ubuntu-latest) 1), the three the issue already recorded and no fourth, with one listing unread and named. ⛔ Its mutation sweep found the suite reaching the real GitHub for 4 min 25 s with a refusal deleted, because the flag table’s only protection from the network was the guard under test; the reader is a variable the tests replace now.
secretscan (v0.157.0) finds the daemons that take a secret as a plaintext value: a config-struct field, a cobra or pflag flag, an os.Getenv name, a systemd Environment= or ExecStart flag, a launchd plist, instead of by reference (a go-authn/secretsource *_from such as systemd-creds:name). A name is judged by its words, never a substring: token_file is a path, password_from a reference, max_tokens and key_file are not secrets, and a flag whose default is a path (~/.github-token) or whose usage says file or path is a path. secretscan sweep --root --json out.json --md out.md reads every clone, opens its report with the denominator (clones seen, read, skipped; files read, unread), counts daemons and findings per repository by canonical origin URL so the worktrees of one repository count once, and exits 2 when anything was skipped or unreadable: an unread clone is NOT READ, never clean. secretscan repo [--waive ""] [--all] CLONE is the gate for one repository (exit 1 on a plaintext input of a daemon). A flow into os.Open or a *From reader is not followed, and a main that only calls a library server is found through its unit file or not at all.
renovatedup (v0.159.0; its GraphQL budget guard in v0.161.0) finds the repositories that apply their organisation’s Renovate preset twice. When /.github/config.js sets inheritConfig, Renovate merges the inherited file into every repository and then also reads the repository’s own config, so a renovate.json whose extends names that same file registers every custom manager twice (measured on go-crdt, go-crdt/.github#45: the dashboards went from regex (4) to (2) once the stubs were removed). renovatedup [--orgs ORG,...] reads each organisation in one GraphQL query per 100 repositories, with the .github config.js and every candidate config file in Renovate’s search order, and reports STUB (the file holds only that extends: remove the file), MIXED (other rules too: remove only the entry) or UNREAD (a JSON5, truncated or unparsable file, or a failed organisation query). Exit 0 is clean, 1 a duplicate, 2 something unread, and 2 outranks 1. Measured with v0.161.0 on 2026-11-22: go-crdt 1 STUB (go-crdt/brand, a recorded exception), go-composites 34 STUB out of 34 repositories. Since v0.161.0 the shared budget guard charges a GraphQL call to the GraphQL budget, so the sweep still runs when the REST budget is spent.
orgfile (v0.156.0, #401) reads one file from each organisation’s .github repository, or from the first of --repos that has it, and says whether it contains each --contains string. GitHub code search does not index these files, so each is read through the REST contents endpoint, about one call per organisation. One verdict per organisation: match (every string present), nomatch (the line says which is absent), nofile (404 on every repository) or unread (any other status, never read as nofile). ⛔ It stops cleanly when REST remaining falls below --reserve (default 1000) and says every count is then a floor; a run that read nothing never prints a clean result. --orgs narrows, --workers sets concurrency, --list prints every organisation. Exit 0 every organisation read, 1 some unread or stopped at the reserve, 2 usage error or could not start.
orgedit (v0.162.0, #422; resume fix in v0.163.0, #424) rolls one literal replacement in one file out to every organisation, as one pull request per organisation, merged only when CI is green. Its first use is #305: replacing --package renovate@latest with --package renovate@44 in each organisation’s .github/workflows/ci.yml. Per organisation the file is read once and judged nofile, unchanged, skip (it contains a --skip-if string) or target; any other answer is unread, counted and never read as nofile. A target is handled one at a time: the REST --reserve must hold and the trailing hour must have fewer than --max merged pull requests (default 20), or the run stops; a repository another session holds is skipped and listed; a leftover branch or an open pull request from an earlier run is resumed, never doubled; the pull request is opened, waited on with prwait, and merged with ghmerge only when the checks, read again against the pushed commit, are green. A red or inconclusive CI, a refused command, the reserve and the cap each stop the run, and nothing is retried another way. --dry-run reads only and prints each verdict with the diff size. Exit 0 every organisation read and every target merged or skipped, 1 a refusal, a red CI or an unread file, 2 usage error or a limit reached.
The two added since the 86, both on 2026-11-15, are editurl and recur. editurl asks whether a Hextra site’s “Edit this page on GitHub” link reaches the page’s own source, and reads the repository rather than the URL: GitHub’s /edit/ route authenticates before it resolves a path, so an anonymous request to an existing repository answers 302 to a login page whatever the path is, and a fetcher cannot tell a correct href from a broken one. Measured over 1318 checkouts: 75 of the 97 sites that render the link do not resolve — 64 name a repository that does not exist (github.com//edit/…), 7 name the organisation’s code repository rather than its docs one, and 4 double the language (…/content/en/en/page.md). recur refuses to publish while a lesson that recorded a recurrence has no gate.
statecheck (v0.177.0) is a Claude Code Stop hook for a reply that states the current state of an external system (a quota exhausted, an App installed, a runner blocked) or asks the user to change one, when no tool call of the turn read it: a note or a summary is history with no read time. Grouped by the question they answer:
Is the fleet green? redscan (every default branch whose last run failed — a red branch is not a broken one, check when it last ran), quietscan, prscan, prmerge, glmerge (the GitLab side), relverify, cronscan.
Can this pull request still go green? prrefresh (updates a pull request branch with its base and names the ones it could not — a pull request in conflict with its base gets no workflow run at all, not a failing one, so it keeps its last green and reads as ready). It sends expected_head_sha, so it refuses rather than merges into a head that moved under it, and it treats GitHub’s mergeable: null as “the background job has not finished” rather than as a refusal — reading null as false reports a conflict for every pull request asked about too soon.
Is what is merged reachable, and is the version right? tagscan (a module whose branch is ahead of its latest tag: work that is merged and go get cannot reach — it asks about tags, not releases), vscan (what the next version should be, derived from the public API with gorelease, once per GOOS), tagcells, gorequires, pinscan, modrename.
Is there work nobody can find? branchscan (branches holding commits the default branch does not have that no pull request was ever opened for). Such a branch is invisible to gh pr list and to any backlog that tracks issues, so it does not read as abandoned — it reads as absent, and the work gets done a second time. The cousin of tagscan: that one finds work merged and unreachable, this one finds work nobody ever saw. priorart asks the same question from the other end, about a subject rather than a population, and before the work starts: given a repository and a subject it reads the branches — by name and head-commit subject, since a branch is named for its mechanism and its commit written for its cause — and the issues and pull requests, open and closed, and exits non-zero when the subject is already covered. No is:open qualifier, deliberately: a closed “not merged, and here is why” is the most valuable prior art there is. It exists because three pieces of work were redone on one repository in a single day while “search the tracker first” was already written down as a rule — the thought arrives as let me fix this, never as let me check whether this is fixed, so the check runs instead of being remembered. A surface it could not read holds the gate shut (status 2) even when another surface found something — and that clause was the defect rather than the design: found was tested before unread, so a branch match returned “already covered” on a run whose tracker had answered HTTP 422 and been read by nobody, printing the warning above a verdict that said the opposite. The shut gate includes a GraphQL refusal, which arrives as HTTP 200 with an errors array: read past that and a refused query becomes an empty branch list, which is a clean gate on a surface never read.
-all-orgs widens the question from one repository to the account. On 2026-11-26 a search of one repository could not see cloud-boot/windows-image, cloud-boot/iso or go-diskimages, which already covered the subject. One call now searches the tracker (open and closed) of every organisation the account belongs to and reports per organisation: those with entries one by one, the clean ones in a single line. The list is GitHub’s /user/orgs, the one -deps already reads, rather than a committed file, which would drift from the real fleet. Searches are spaced for the search limit of 30 a minute. An organisation whose search failed is NOT READ, and an unreadable or empty list is one surface not read: status 2, never “no organisation has it”. It combines with -repo.
The search is split at six terms, because GitHub allows five AND/OR/NOT operators and seven OR-ed clauses answered HTTP 422 outright — so the subjects that silently lost the tracker half were the carefully written ones, which are the subjects most likely to have prior art. Terms are batched six to a query and the results unioned; one failed batch is the whole surface unread, not a partial answer. Splitting costs the single global ranking, since GitHub ranks within a query, so batches are emitted in term order and each keeps the order the search gave it — nothing re-ranks them, because a scoring pass of its own was measured against GitHub’s relevance and came out worse.
Does the CI actually test it? testscan, judgescan (tests that look for an external tool the CI never installs — a foreign judge that exists in the source and has never once run), covblocks (the blocks a coverage profile never entered, because go tool cover -func rounds to one decimal and a 100 % gate passes at 99.95 %), buildscan, buildtag, flagcensus, runson (which runner images the workflows ask for, counted per repository and not per file: 1226 of 1247 checkouts with workflows stand on ubuntu-latest, which upstream is moving to Ubuntu 26.04 between 2026-10-19 and 2026-11-19 — inside that window a red CI can be the image moving while the repository did not). ⛔ It reads checkouts and makes no API call, and the price of reading a disk is stated rather than disclaimed: it measures how many of the checkouts it read are behind their remote — 842 of 1247, furthest 188 commits, with 405 more never fetched within the horizon, so not one is confirmed current — and says which way that makes it wrong, because a checkout predating a newly added workflow makes the count a floor and an absence read off a stale disk looks exactly like a real one.
Is it safe? vulnscan, vulngate (the per-repository half), gofloor (which Go toolchain a repository can be built with, and whether CI would notice a vulnerable one), wfaudit, blobpurge, needread (the DT_NEEDED entries of every ELF under a tree, refusing to report unless a symbol it was told to expect is actually there), symfind (whether an ELF exports a dynamic symbol, rather than merely consuming it).
Is it advertised, and is the page what it builds? docscan, docscheck (which generator a published URL was built with), pagescheck (whether a Pages site serves what its repository builds), pagetext (whether a published page now carries the text we wrote), sitelinks (whether every local link of a built site leads to a file of that build), editurl (whether a Hextra site’s “Edit this page on GitHub” link reaches the page’s own source — it reads the repository, because that link’s status code cannot tell a correct href from a broken one), linkcheck (whether every external link a documentation source names still resolves — it replaced the grep/sed/curl the documentation workflows carried, which failed twice on random 504s from github.com and passed on the third run), docsym, i18ncheck, langcheck, mantracheck, brandcheck.
Speaking to something that is not GitHub. bzcomment posts one comment to a Bugzilla bug through its REST API, showing which bug and which account it is about to speak for first. It exists so a session can contribute upstream without the API key ever passing through a URL, an argument vector, the environment or a log.
Publishing the documentation. pagespublish, pagesretire, mkdocs2hextra, sitemigrate, landingmigrate, docsversions (every published version of a versioned site built with one look — the default branch’s), mdpdf.
What does it cost, and on what? wasmsize, hostload, abbench, truncspill, gvlscan, gopin, qemufix. Since v0.71.0 abbench also runs on macOS and can compare two sub-benchmarks of one binary: --max-load F --wait D waits for the 1-minute load to be at most F before each round and discards a round’s pair when the load after it is above F, so the two series stay paired; --base-arg and --head-arg add arguments to one side, and --rename-base / --rename-head give the two sub-benchmarks one name so that benchstat base.txt head.txt compares them (benchstat keys rows by full name). The load reading is the public package github.com/go-fleettools/fleettools/loadavg (Avg1, Wait), also used by go-llmflow/bench’s gwbench.
Comparing artefacts. treecmp (byte for byte), pngeq (the same pixels, because “65 of 73 files differ” on a moved brand kit was false — 51 PNGs, 0 channel values different).
The small ones. brief (runs a command, shows the end of what it said, and keeps its exit status), unarc, truncspill, clonescan.
data.flags#Flags: one dash became two:
Since v0.53.0 all of the commands use cobra, so the canonical spelling is --long with POSIX short forms. The fleet had typed -dir, -apply, -org for months, and pflag reads one dash as one letter, so every one of those would have been refused: a single-dash compatibility shim in internal/cli rewrites the old spelling and warns, which is why there was no flag day. cmd/flagcensus is the measurement that drove it — 54 commands, 144 flags, 137 of which needed the second dash.
⛔⛔ And this repository’s own workflows kept typing one dash for another year’s worth of runs. v0.82.1 fixed eight call sites in two files — vulngate -go, vulnscan -selftest twice, three more vulnscan lines, and brandcheck -org — every one of them invoking a binary built from that very tree, so cobra, so the shim was the only thing making them work. The shim prints a warning on every run and announces its own removal: a warning inside a green lane is a warning nobody reads, and the day the shim goes those lanes fail for a reason unrelated to anything they measure.
Seven were found by another session and routed here through two lease notes. The eighth was found by the test written for the other seven, on its first run, in a file nobody had looked at — TestNoWorkflowCallsOurOwnCommandsWithASingleDash, which enumerates cmd/ rather than naming the commands, refuses to run if it sees no workflow or implausibly few commands, scans only after the command’s own token (so go build -o /tmp/vulnscan is not a call), and skips comments — its first version flagged a line of prose describing a hole its author had already removed, and refusing what the protected thing accepts is a defect of the same rank as missing one. modfloor v0.8.1 carries the narrow version of the same gate, because its security lane had the defect too.
data.fleettools#fleettools:
Sweeps across about 1800 repositories and about 320 organisations: which default branches are red, which runners stopped or run and fail, which modules are ahead of their tag, which foreign judges the CI never installs, and which tests exist without ever running. Repository → Latest tag: v0.161.0 (740afd7, read on 2026-11-22 with git ls-remote --tags … refs/tags/v0.161.0, which is also how tagcells resolves it — the commit is read from the tag, never carried over from the previous one). The prose below was written from the repository at v0.67.0, plus the two v0.82.x sections and the modtidy section at the end written from the change itself — the command inventory under cmd/, the README’s own sections, and each new command’s doc comment — and the two are kept apart on purpose: which tag is current and which tag this page describes are different facts, and writing one where the other belongs is how a page comes to assert a version it was never checked against. The README is about 610 lines and describes every command in its own words; read it there.
The sweeps were written on 2026-08-30 while getting every default branch green, and the README says why each one is built the way it is. The repository has one directory per sweep under cmd/; the module is github.com/go-fleettools/fleettools, and a command is installed the way Go installs tools, at a tag (go install github.com/go-fleettools/fleettools/cmd/vulngate@v0.81.2).
data.modtidy#modtidy: every go.mod of a clone:
Written from the change at v0.123.0 (4235455), not from the README.
go mod tidy at the root does not enter a directory that has its own go.mod. Three recorded occurrences, each a root that was tidied and tested green before the CI went red with “updates to go.mod needed”: go-widgets/toolkit twice, through its rougelex/ sub-module, and go-numerics/integrate through bench/. So modtidy [dir] finds every go.mod beneath a clone and judges each one with GOTOOLCHAIN=local GOWORK=off go mod tidy -diff — the CI’s own constraint, because GOTOOLCHAIN=auto fetches whatever a directive asks for and hides the problem, and a go.work file would let a sibling satisfy a requirement the CI never sees. modtidy --hook is the PreToolUse form: it acts only on a command position gitpush or git push, and denies the push naming the module and the fix.
A module is reported tidy, untidy with its diff, UNREAD, or skipped.
⛔ UNREAD is never clean, and the two classes below exist because the command twice gave an answer where it could not know. Both were measured on 2026-11-15.
data.modtidy-floor#A directive floor above th:
GOTOOLCHAIN=local is the right constraint to reproduce, but on a host whose installed Go is older than a module’s go line it cannot build the module at all — and in the hook, UNREAD means allow. The gate had therefore gone silently off for every repository raised to go 1.27.4, this one included:
UNREAD .: go: go.mod requires go >= 1.27.4 (running go 1.27.3; GOTOOLCHAIN=local) The check now retries once with the toolchain the directive names, which reproduces the CI rather than loosening anything: the runner there has the version the directive requires, which is the only reason GOTOOLCHAIN=local succeeds for it. Deliberately not GOTOOLCHAIN=auto, which leaves the version used unstated — an instrument whose version is implicit is not an instrument. GOWORK=off is untouched. The report names the toolchain that answered, so a verdict reached under the directive’s version can be told from one reached under whatever the host happens to have installed.
⛔ A broken go.mod is still UNREAD, never skipped: a skip is a clean answer, and “holds no .go file” has not read the file that is wrong. The repository’s own corpus caught that during the change — a go.mod holding garbage has no Go source beside it either.
data.modtidy-nosource#A module with no Go sou:
go-fft/docs is a Hugo site whose only requirement is its theme. Running the remedy the hook itself printed — "go mod tidy, commit go.mod and go.sum" — empties both files and the site loses its theme. A gate that instructs the next session to break the repository is worse than no gate.
In a module with no Go source, a tidy can only ever remove requirements, so its verdict carries no information. Such a module is skipped, with the reason named, decided before go runs at all — no toolchain, no network.
Three details are the fix rather than decoration:
A Hugo configuration is reported, never what decides. go-fft/docs has no [module] block; it mounts its theme with theme = ["…"]. A rule keyed on that block would have missed the one repository it was written for. A nested module’s sources never answer for its parent, or a Hugo site with a small Go tool beside it reads as Go code. A file behind a build constraint still counts. A //go:build tools file holding a blank import is the documented way to keep a requirement no package uses, and skipping such a module would have hidden two dead go.sum lines this gate correctly found in a landing. ⚠ And the pattern the fleet already documents cannot repair such a repository instead: go mod tidy reports “module … found, but does not contain package github.com/McShelby/hugo-theme-relearn”. A landing kit is an importable Go package; a Hugo theme is templates and CSS that merely carry a go.mod. There is no package to import, so no Go code can hold that requirement — and nothing in the shape of the two repositories announces the difference.
data.openfixed#openfixed: open issues a merge: openfixed --org A --org B (or --owner) lists open issues that a merged pull request already addressed, so they can be closed. For each owner it searches open issues (the ones with a closing reference, linked:pr, first) and reads each issue’s timeline once. CLOSABLE means a merged pull request referenced the issue with a closing keyword (or the timeline records it as connected) yet it is open; REVIEW means a merged pull request mentioned it with no keyword at all, or the issue was reopened after the merge, so a person decides; REFS means a merged pull request wrote Refs (or Ref), which says the issue stays open on purpose. Issues whose pull requests are all unmerged are not listed. The report states its denominator per owner (issues searched, timelines read, issues skipped and why) and exits 2 if anything was skipped: a scan that could not read is never reported as zero. It is a dry run by default; --close closes only CLOSABLE issues, with a comment naming the pull request, and never a REVIEW or REFS one. It stops before the REST budget falls under --margin (default 1000) so the fleet’s Renovate runners are not starved, and it paces the search API. Written against GitHub’s documented search qualifiers, the issue timeline events and the closing-keyword rules.
data.openfixed-refs#Why REFS is a third word:
Until 2026-11-22, REVIEW meant two unrelated things: nobody has said what becomes of this issue and somebody said, in writing, that it stays open. The fleet-wide merge rule made the second one mandatory — ghmerge refuses a merge whose body mentions an issue and classifies it as neither closed nor kept — so every correctly written Refs #N became permanent REVIEW output. One organisation’s REVIEW held 37 of its 64 open issues, in a bucket whose name means a person decides, and nobody reads such a bucket (go-fleettools/fleettools#204).
A REFS row is still printed, because an author can write Refs and be wrong, and an issue reopened after the merge still deserves a look. What changed is that it is counted apart and sorted last, after the rows that still need a decision — the order carries the meaning, and it is the only part of this that no count could hold: a hand-applied mutation swapping the two ranks left every total correct and moved only the order, and exactly one assertion went red.
⛔ See #N is not one. The gate’s keywords are close/fix/resolve and ref(s), and see #12 is the phrasing the merge gate exists to refuse — it reads as a decision and is not one. The issue asked for Refs and See to be read alike; doing that would have silenced the audit for exactly the sentence the fleet rejects at merge time. Both spellings are negative controls in the test table now.
⛔ The reading is the merge gate’s own parser, issuegate.Parse, which answers closes, refs or bare in one call. A private second regexp for Refs would be a new way for the audit and the gate to disagree — which is how a heading “## Also filed, not fixed” once bound to a reference two lines below it.
data.privscan#privscan: a tool and a door aga:
On 2026-11-09 three issues were filed whose bodies each carried /Users//Documents//.tex — a home directory, an account name, a directory layout and the name of an unpublished document. Nobody noticed until the owner of that machine asked whether their name had been leaked. The rule set afterwards names three things, not one: no leak of a name, nor of a path or a file name, on a user’s file system.
⛔ An edit does not undo it. GitHub keeps the original under edited for anyone who opens the history, so the only complete remedy is to delete and re-create — which is why ghissue --delete exists, and why the gate has to run before the send rather than after.
privscan body.md checks a file; --fix rewrites it; --repo owner/name and --org NAME read what is already published, comments and titles included, because a code search does not index comments reliably — the first sweep of this leak found one occurrence and could not have found a second in a comment. Three paginated repository-wide calls read everything, against one call per issue. A repository whose read failed exits 2 and is never printed as clean.
A finding prints its line, column and kind but not the text it matched unless --show asks: a refusal is printed where the body was going, and that is sometimes a public CI log.
data.privscan-gate#The gate, inside ghissue a:
Since v0.129.0 the gate lives in internal/privgate, shared by ghissue and ghpr, and ghpr create --head BRANCH --title T --body-file F (--base-branch is the target; --base stays the API URL) opens a pull request through it: it also refuses a head with no commits ahead, a head that already has an open pull request, and a body whose issue references lack Closes/Refs.
Every body and title ghissue and ghpr send passes privpath first, in readBody and checkTitle — the two functions every path through the command goes through — with the waiver as a parameter of both, so no future subcommand can read outgoing text without the compiler asking what to do about a disclosure. A gate reached by remembering to call it is not a gate.
--allow-private-path "" takes a reason and has no default: a boolean waiver is one keystroke and gets passed by reflex, while a reason has to be written, and writing it is the moment to notice there is nothing to write. It stamps — the reason is appended to the published text, so a waiver is a statement made in public rather than a switch flicked in private. No waiver covers a title: a title cannot carry the stamp and is republished in every listing, notification and cross-reference that an edit never reaches.
data.privscan-measured#What the first sweep a:
509 findings over 60 repositories — and almost all of them were the instrument, not the fleet. Reading one real body settled it, where no reading of the count could have:
run findings what reading the text removed 1 509 in 67 texts a package manager’s /home/.zpkg/… prefix read as a person called .zpkg, every package name along it then hunted as that person’s document; and a TeX \\ — a line break in LaTeX, an escaped backslash in every Go string — matched as a Windows share whose one-letter name was hunted through all 60 repositories 2 126 in 51 texts /Users/Shared, which is everyone’s; and Home/End/Space, a list of keyboard keys, read as the home directory of a person called End 3 45 in 6 texts — The single real disclosure was the same in all three runs: the one the first sweep had already found. A three-figure count from a new instrument on a large corpus measures the instrument.
⛔ Hence --accounts, which answers the question a count cannot: whose file system was named, and whether this machine’s is among them. The verdict is a sentence, not a number, and a clean sweep prints it too — silence after a sweep reads as clean and cannot be told from a command that printed nothing.
⛔ And hence four sentences for four states of “who am I”, which CI had to teach: --no-self (not checked), an unreadable home, a generic account (/home/runner identifies nobody, so there is nothing of its own to disclose), and a real one. The first version printed “could not be read” for the generic case, which was false — an instrument whose two outcomes read alike measures neither — and computed a verdict about an account --no-self had excluded.
Two design costs are stated on purpose. A generic account’s path is skipped whole, tail included, so a document name under /home/user/ goes unreported; and nothing below a dot-directory is hunted bare, because /Users//.pkgx/llvm.org/v22.1.8/bin/clang-22 taught the scanner llvm.org and v22.1.8 — public package coordinates named six times in the prose that was the report, which a redaction would have eaten.
data.quietscan#quietscan:
quietscan is every organisation whose Renovate runner has stopped, runs and fails, or asks for a secret that does not exist. redscan asks whether the last run failed; a runner that stopped does not fail, it says nothing — so this asks when it last ran, and then what became of it. Sixteen runners were once reported healthy while every nightly run failed in ten seconds, which is the second half the README added.
Since v0.66.0 it also reads the secrets a workflow references against the ones that exist and reports missing_secret with the name, because the sixteen were all one absent RENOVATE_TOKEN and an unset secret expands to the empty string — so the action runs with nothing there and fails in ten seconds, which reads as activity to any check that only asks whether runs happen. That check cannot live inside the workflow: GitHub’s documentation states that secrets cannot be referenced in if: conditionals, and the documented workaround would put a credential in an environment variable to learn something that needs no value. It found its first real one on 2026-11-07 — a runner created six days earlier whose secret was never placed, caught in a day rather than the ten the sixteen took.
The README devotes sections to it: “What quietscan is, and the seven rules it will not soften”, attribution (“the property belongs to whatever COVERS the repository”), “The trap quietscan exists to catch before it latches”, “A failed call must never become a verdict”, “What one pass costs, and when not to run it”, and “Two things quietscan is not”. Read them there before scheduling it beside another sweep.
data.reusable#The reusable workflows:
Three checks here are called by the repository they guard, so they fail where the change is made rather than in a report nobody opens — nine lines in the caller, and ⛔ not on: [push, pull_request], which both fire for a branch with a pull request open and doubled every run on the first three organisations that copied the snippet.
docs-current.yml does this organisation advertise what it has? Needs no secret: listing a public organisation is a public read brand-complete.yml does a brand repository carry what its README promises? Written because a brand repository has nothing to compile, so it had no checks at all and ghmerge rightly refused its pull requests go-floor.yml (v0.82.0) does this branch declare a go directive at or above the fleet’s floor? ⛔ go-floor.yml exists because the fleet-wide sweep structurally cannot catch its case. modfloor --baseline answers did anything get worse, and a repository created below the floor arrives as new to the population, where nothing says whether it was ever clean. Measured over the five days to 2026-11-07: 0 regressed, 14 fixed, 61 arrived exposed — the fleet’s exposure went 262 → 314 without one regression. Its floor: input is required, because a default would move under every caller with no commit to review, which is the go-version: stable defect this fleet spent a campaign removing; it pins the judging tool to a tag rather than a branch, since a gate that fails builds must not change what hundreds of repositories are held to with nothing reviewed; and --offline means it reads the working tree, so there is no API call and no secret.

data.audit#fuzzrun audit:
fuzzrun audit [--dir .] Finds the fuzz targets no workflow fuzzes. It parses the test files for the FuzzXxx targets, as run does, reads .github/workflows/*.yml, and prints a GAP per target no step fuzzes and a BLANKET per fuzz step under continue-on-error: true — a step that cannot fail cannot say that nothing was fuzzed. A step running fuzzrun run covers every target, or those of its --package. The program is any shell word whose last path element is fuzzrun, quoted or not — fuzzrun, "$(go env GOPATH)/bin/fuzzrun", go run github.com/go-fleettools/fuzzrun@vX run — and echo "fuzzrun run", a # … fuzzrun run comment or xfuzzrun run are not calls. ⛔ Up to v0.7.0 a regular expression read it, and was wrong both ways: a quoted path was no call, so its targets came out GAP (go-crdt/crdt#185’s first version), and the three non-calls above read as covering every target — a false green. Otherwise only a go test -fuzz that go test would really run counts: the pattern is an unanchored regexp, a pattern matching more than one target of the package fuzzes none, and -fuzz over several packages is refused by the go tool; those steps are NOTEs and their targets stay gaps.
A static strategy.matrix is expanded anywhere in the step’s script — the -fuzz pattern and the package operand — because a matrix lane names them together: -fuzz '^${{ matrix.target }}$' ${{ matrix.pkg }}. Up to v0.5.0 only the pattern was expanded, so the package stayed literal, the step read as computed at run time, and every target it covers came out UNCERTAIN. Measured on go-crdt/crdt, whose fuzz lane is twenty static include entries:
v0.5.0 35 targets, 0 without a workflow, 35 uncertain, exit 0 v0.6.0 35 targets, 0 without a workflow, 15 uncertain, exit 0 The 15 that remain are a lane whose pattern a shell loop builds from a grep, which no reader of the file can decide (go-crdt/crdt#184 asks that repository whether to make it readable).
⛔ The combinations are paired, not crossed. The list keys give the cross product, exclude removes what it matches, and each include entry is a job of its own, so twenty entries pairing a package with a target stay twenty jobs rather than becoming sixty. Coverage is keyed by (package, target), and an invented job would mark a target covered whenever the same target name exists in another package — the one answer an audit must never produce. A matrix holding both a list and include is not a pairing the audit reads: the two are crossed and a NOTE says so.
A step the audit cannot read — a pattern the shell computes, make fuzz, a script, a working-directory — makes the uncovered targets UNCERTAIN instead of GAP, and they do not fail the audit — unless every target is uncertain.
Exit status: 0 everything covered, or some covered and the rest uncertain, 1 gaps or a blanket continue-on-error, 2 nothing could be read, including every target uncertain. ⛔ Up to v0.7.2 that last case exited 0: nothing was decided, the summary’s 0 without a workflow was true and empty, and a lane running the audit stayed green over a workflow it could not read — go-crdt/crdt’s 35 of 35 above. go-fleettools/fuzzrun#14 raised the question; since v0.8.0 it is exit 2, as wfaudit and redscan do for a scan that read nothing, because an answer not obtained is not a negative. A partly uncertain module still exits 0: at least one target was read as covered, and the UNCERTAIN lines name the rest.
data.fuzzrun#fuzzrun:
Run every Go fuzz target of a module, in parallel within a load budget, and report crashers. Repository → Latest tag: v0.9.0 (go list -m -versions, 2026-11-22). This page describes wait from the README at v0.1.0, audit from the README at v0.8.0 and run from the README at v0.7.0, and the versions are stated separately on purpose: which tag is current and which tag this page describes are different facts. ⚠ The repository also has census, workflow and adopt subcommands, which this page does not describe yet — they are named here so their absence reads as a gap and not as a tool that lacks them.
go test -fuzz runs one target of one package at a time, so a module with thirty targets needs thirty commands, and a run left unattended either overloads the machine or leaves it idle. fuzzrun finds the targets, runs a few at once, waits for the machine to be quiet enough before starting each one, keeps one log per target, and says in a summary which target crashed and where the corpus file that reproduces it was written.
data.run#fuzzrun run:
fuzzrun run [--dir .] [--time 10m] [--jobs 3] [--parallel 2] \ [--max-load 0] [--logs DIR] [--package pattern...] Targets are found by parsing the *_test.go files (go/parser, not a regular expression): top-level func FuzzXxx(f *testing.F). .git and testdata are skipped, and a test file that does not parse is an error, never silently zero targets. Each target runs as go test -run=^$ -fuzz=^Name$ -fuzztime=D -parallel=P ./pkg with GOWORK=off, at most --jobs at a time, its output in /-.log. --max-load L (L > 0): before starting each target, wait while the 1-minute load average is above L. It is read from sysctl vm.loadavg on darwin and /proc/loadavg on linux. Where it cannot be read, run exits 2 up front instead of pretending the machine was quiet. --package keeps only matching packages (repeatable). A target that fails with a Failing input written to testdata/fuzz// line is a CRASH, and the summary gives that path relative to the module. Since v0.7.0, a target that fails with context deadline exceeded and wrote no failing input is a DEADLINE: the fuzz coordinator’s own deadline arrived while a worker was still inside an input, with nothing found. It is printed with its log and counted, and it does not make the run exit 1. The crasher is checked first — a target can reach the deadline after writing a failing input, and is then a CRASH. Any other failing exit is a FAIL, with the log to read. PASS ./. FuzzGood 5s CRASH ./. FuzzBad 1.2s testdata/fuzz/FuzzBad/6f1c... DEADLINE ./. FuzzSlow 30.4s (exit status 1; log …/root-FuzzSlow.log) 3 targets: 1 PASS, 0 FAIL, 1 CRASH, 1 DEADLINE Exit status: 0 every target passed or reached the deadline, 1 at least one FAIL or CRASH, 2 the run could not be made (no go.mod, no targets, go missing, bad flags, unreadable load with --max-load).
⛔ Before v0.7.0 the deadline was a FAIL, so exit 1 could not tell a crash from weather and a lane using run had to choose between going red on the deadline and tolerating exit 1 — which keeps it green on a real crasher. A lane that wanted “a crash is red, a deadline warns” had to keep its own shell loop (go-crdt/crdt#184 is that case). The DEADLINE count is appended after CRASH, so a parser of the older line keeps reading it.
data.wait#fuzzrun wait: fuzzrun wait FILE SUBSTRING [--timeout 10m] [--interval 2s] Blocks until FILE contains SUBSTRING, for example a log written by a background fuzzrun run. It prints found (exit 0) or timeout (exit 1); exit 2 on a read error other than the file not existing yet.
data.why#Why: The fuzz targets of a module are a security control only if they are actually run, all of them, for long enough, without taking the machine down. The tool came out of the go-llmflow/gateway security audit, where thirty targets were run by hand with a shell loop that could not tell a crash from a timeout. Its tests plant a failing target and require run to report it with its corpus path and exit 1; the module is copied to a temporary directory first, so the corpus a crash writes never lands in the repository.

data.landingdiff#landingdiff:
Which of a set of landing pages is the odd one out, by counting what each page puts in the shared design system. Repository → Latest tag: v0.3.0 (git ls-remote --tags, 2026-11-15); this page is written from its README at v0.2.0, and the two are stated separately on purpose: which tag is current and which tag this page describes are different facts. The README at the tag this page describes gives no install line; one was added on main on 2026-10-26, after checking that it builds:
go install github.com/go-fleettools/landingdiff@latest landingdiff ../landing-go-*/layouts/index.html go-authn go-fileshare go-pkgx go-pdfkit spread headline line 1, characters 14 10 19 23 10..23 items in the trust band 3 3 3 4 3..4 <- go-pdfkit buttons in the hero 2 2 2 2 ... go-pdfkit is alone on 2 measure(s) (An excerpt of the README’s example.)
data.limits#What it will not tell you: A page is named only when the others agree and it does not: one value held by everybody else, one page holding something different. It deliberately does not flag “furthest from the rest”, which would name the smallest and the largest every time. It is blind to layout. A headline too long for its column is a fact about rendering, found by screenshotting the pages; use both, because neither finds the other’s. Read the comment on the line before you “fix” an outlier: an outlier the history explains is not drift. To add a measure, add one entry in measures: a name and a function from the page’s HTML to a count, returning -1, not 0, when the part is not there at all.
data.why#Why counting, and not diffing: The landings share one styles.html, so “aligned” cannot be checked by diffing the design system. What drifts is what each page puts in it: a band with one more item than fits on a line, a navigation with twice as many links as its neighbours.

data.brand#landingkit brand: landingkit brand static/img/logo.svg >> hugo.toml # then remove the old block The brand colour is read from the logo’s gradient, never chosen, and it is the only thing an organisation sets: the first two stop-color of the SVG give a dark stop (base, which carries text on white) and a light one (bright, the accent in dark mode), and every other value is derived. data.baseline#--baseline: a gate for a campai:
⛔ A report that is red for ever is not a gate. 262 published modules declare a floor below 1.27.3, so modfloor --floor 1.27.3 exits 1 every time it runs and will keep doing so for as long as raising them takes. A lane in that state is read as broken, then ignored — and the day a new module lands below the floor, nothing changes colour.
modfloor --dir … --owners 'go-*' --floor 1.27.3 --write-baseline floor.txt modfloor --dir … --owners 'go-*' --floor 1.27.3 --baseline floor.txt --baseline exits 1 only for a module the recorded set does not have. The file is plain text so a tightened baseline has a readable diff, and it names the floor and the mode it was taken against.
Refused Why no floor line, or another floor every verdict changes the day the floor moves, and it moved three times in four days (1.27.1 → 1.27.2 → 1.27.3). A set of module names says nothing without the floor it was judged against another mode --offline records what the working trees declare, the default what the proxy serves: different answers about the same modules --baseline and --write-baseline recording the answer and then judging it against itself always passes, which is a gate that cannot fail The file records every module the run measured, clean ones included, and says so with a records all line; a baseline without it (anything v0.6.1 wrote) is refused.
⛔⛔ The clean ones are the point, and the first version left them out. It fired 80 minutes after its own baseline with “8 module(s) are exposed that the baseline did not have” — every one a repository another session had just cloned, one of them appearing on disk a minute before the run, the population growing from 348 modules to 360. A clone arriving is not the fleet getting worse. And the silent half is the dangerous one: with only the exposed set recorded, a module that was ok and is exposed now cannot be told from one never measured, so the real regression would have been filed as population growth and the gate would have passed.
Four outcomes, and only the first fails a run:
WORSE the baseline measured it and found it clean; it is exposed now. The gate new to the population (not a regression) exposed, and the baseline never measured it. Work, but nothing says it was ever clean. ⚠ A repository created below the floor arrives this way too, which only a check in its own CI can catch fixed was exposed, measured again, no longer exposed NOT MEASURED THIS TIME (not a fix) was exposed and did not appear at all — clone deleted, renamed, out of the owner globs, or simply not walked. A vanished subject looks exactly like a repaired one to anything that only subtracts two sets, and adding them together is how a campaign declares victory by losing track of its subjects ⭐ The baseline is also what caught the wrong population above. The report prints 348 rows and a summary, and nobody reads 348 rows; the baseline writes the exposed set to a file as a sorted list of module paths, where cel.dev/expr two lines from the top is impossible to miss.
⚠ Where it should run is not settled: a baseline is a statement about one machine’s clone population, so committing one in the repository would make its lane depend on that machine.
data.cost#A campaign is costed in pull reques:
⛔ “262 modules below the floor” reads as 262 pieces of work, and it is not: several modules of one repository are raised by one pull request, because the go directives they declare land together. On a sibling campaign 896 stale CI pins turned out to be 123 pull requests — a factor of seven — and an estimate seven times too large is an estimate that gets the campaign refused.
⛔ And the size is not the shape. gopin --gomod --from X --version Y names the version to move exactly — deliberately, because “move anything older” cannot tell a stale pin from a deliberate hold, and this fleet has removed a deliberate one as an outlier before. So a campaign over modules declaring several floors is one run per floor, and v0.7.0 says which:
they declare 10 different floors, so `gopin --gomod --from X --version 1.27.3` is 10 runs and not one: --from 1.27.1 191 --from 1.26.4 4 --from 1.24 1 --from 1.27.2 61 --from 1.26.0 1 --from 1.21 1 --from 1.27.0 3 --from 1.25 1 --from (none) 3 --from 1.27 3 Two runs cover 252 of the 262. A module with no directive at all is grouped under (none), because --from has nothing to match there. The floors are ordered as Go versions and never as text, since 1.9 is below 1.10 and this list is read by somebody choosing which run to do first.
⛔ Here the pull-request factor is 1.19, not 7: 262 modules in 221 repositories. Said plainly, because it is the second measurement on this page that did not give the answer it was taken for — the first being the published/unpublished split, where all 262 turned out installable. The grouping that saved a sibling campaign seven eighths of its work saves this one nothing much, and 221 pull requests is the real number to decide about.
A module named as a positional argument has no work tree, so there is no repository to credit it to: those are counted apart rather than folded into the estimate, since a module that was not found on disk is one we may not be able to push to at all.

data.modfloor#modfloor:
The Go toolchain floor a module declares, against the floor a fix requires. Repository → Latest tag: v0.13.0 (git ls-remote --tags, 2026-11-22); this page is written from its README at v0.7.0, and the two are stated separately on purpose: which tag is current and which tag this page describes are different facts. v0.3.0 added the modfloor pseudo subcommand, below; v0.4.0 splits the exposure by whether a consumer can reach it, below; v0.5.0 adds --baseline, below, and corrects the population every earlier figure was counted over; v0.6.0 costs the campaign in pull requests, below; v0.7.0 groups it by the floor each module declares and stops the ratchet calling population growth a regression.
A repository can be green, released and built with a patched toolchain while still shipping a vulnerable floor to everyone downstream. Three pins decide three different things: go-version: in a workflow builds the artefacts; the toolchain recorded in a binary says what one installed executable was built with; and the go directive in the published go.mod is what a consumer honours under GOTOOLCHAIN=local. Only the third is the exposure, and no green check looks at it.

data.reads#What it reads, and what it refuses:
It reads the published go.mod from proxy.golang.org, where a consumer reads it too, not the working tree (which may hold an unreleased fix) and not a workflow. It spends no GitHub API budget and needs no credential. --owners is a declared population, and every number in the report is about that set; a module in no git work tree, or under another owner, is set aside and counted. A measurement that found nothing refuses rather than reporting a clean fleet.
⛔ And being in our work tree does not make the module ours — the half that was missing until v0.5.0. remote.origin.url answers “whose repository is this”, not “whose module is this”, and a repository that carries other projects’ sources put 540 of them into this fleet’s figures. A module whose path is not the repository’s own path — github.com//, or a subdirectory or /v2 of it — is set aside as published by another project.
⛔ And a module we publish is still not one anybody installs — the third half, added in v0.13.0. A Hugo landing site is a module with no Go packages: its go.mod exists only to pin a theme module, and nobody runs go install github.com//.github.io, so its floor binds no consumer. The verdict was correct on its own terms and unusable, which is how a column teaches its reader to skim. A module whose own tree holds no .go file an ordinary build could compile is set aside as with no buildable Go package.
Measured on 2026-11-21 over the local clones, offline, against floor 1.27.4, with the check and without it:
without: 12067 go.mod seen, 1253 kept ok=428 BELOW=825 with: 12064 go.mod seen, 914 kept ok=100 BELOW=814 339 modules left the population and only 11 of them were exposures. The other 328 were clean: landing sites are renovated like everything else, so the fleet’s compliance read 34 % clean (428 of 1253) when it was 11 % (100 of 914). Setting them aside took a flattering numerator out of the clean column, not only noise out of the exposure one.
⛔ The test is the packages, never the name. go-pkgx/go-pkgx.github.io ships four Go modules under tools/, so a rule keyed on *.github.io would exempt real code — a false clean rather than noise. A file counts when some ordinary configuration compiles it: //go:build windows counts, foo_arm64.go counts, //go:build tools does not, and //go:build !windows counts even though evaluating it once with windows true says otherwise. The standard-tag set is checked against go tool dist list, because a GOOS missing from it would make a module leave the population silently.
Two traps it encodes: go/version accepts go27.2 (a typo that compares above every real version), so the floor is validated; and modfile.ParseLax does not fill File.Toolchain, so the directive is recovered from the syntax tree.
data.split#The exposure, split by who can rea:
One number over both populations cannot be prioritised. A module on the proxy imposes its floor on everyone who runs go install; one that was never published imposes it only on somebody building from a clone. Those are a campaign and some housekeeping, and until v0.4.0 the report added them together. A third line counts the modules whose working tree is already at the floor and whose published module is not — the fixed locally, UNRELEASED state, where the pull request is merged and the work is not finished, because the consumer reads the published go.mod and not the branch. This tool exists because those two differ, so that state is counted by name instead of waiting in a NOTE column somebody would have to read 939 rows to find.
Measured 2026-11-01, with the population printed beside it, because a count is only as good as the set it counts over:
population: owners go-*,tannevaled — 1789 go.mod seen, 348 kept; set aside: 410 out of scope, 44 in no work tree, 540 published by another project, 0 without a module directive, 0 unreadable 348 modules against floor 1.27.3: ok=86 BELOW=260 no-go=2 ⛔ 262 modules declare a floor below 1.27.3 … they live in 221 repositories, so the campaign is about 221 pull requests and not 262. of those, 262 are PUBLISHED on the proxy (a consumer can install them) and 0 were never published. and 6 already carry the fix in their working tree but have not been RELEASED… ⛔ Worth saying plainly: the split was added because it might have shrunk the campaign, and it did not — all 262 are installable. A measurement earns its place when either answer would change what you do, not only when it gives the answer you hoped for.
⛔⛔ And the figure this page carried for a day was wrong. It said 904 of 939. That count was true over a population that included 540 modules other projects publish, sitting inside our own work trees: sigs.k8s.io/yaml, cel.dev/expr and twenty more, all inside tannevaled/pantry. Every remote.origin.url said tannevaled, so every one passed the owner test, and nobody here can raise the floor of sigs.k8s.io/yaml. v0.5.0 sets them aside and counts them on the population line. The real campaign is 262 modules.
The counting is a named function rather than four variables inside the printer, so it has a test and needs no network. The test plants all five verdicts — including toolchain, which is not an exposure because it fails closed under GOTOOLCHAIN=local — and asserts that published plus unpublished is the whole exposure, so a row drifting out of both buckets cannot shrink the campaign silently.

data.atomic#Nothing is written by truncation:
⛔ A restore on a signal is not enough, and it took a lost file to see it. Measured 2026-11-21: a mutsweep was killed (exit 137 — SIGKILL) while sweeping go-fleettools/prwait, and left quota.go at zero bytes. Not mutated, not half-written: 434 lines gone, and wc -l answering 0. The cause was os.WriteFile, which truncates and then writes — between those two steps the file is empty on disk, and SIGKILL cannot be trapped, so the signal handler that restores on SIGINT could never have covered it. The file happened to be committed, so nothing was lost. An hour of uncommitted work would have been.
Since v0.13.0 every mutation and every restore writes a temporary file in the target’s own directory and renames it over the target, so at each instant the file holds either all of its old contents or all of the new ones, and a kill at any point leaves one or the other. The temporary has to share that directory: a rename across filesystems is a copy and an unlink, which would reintroduce exactly this window while looking like it had closed it. The pattern was already in the repository, in mutsweep/record.go — the ledger was written atomically and the source code was not.
⛔ A swept file keeps the mode it had, and that now takes doing. A rename installs a new inode, which carries the temporary file’s 0o600, so an executable or a group-readable source would have come back private after every mutation. The mode is read off the target and handed back — read once, in the writer, rather than by each caller: the callers that used to stat the file themselves each gained an error path that cannot be reached, since a stat failing after the same file has just been read is a race no test can arrange. mutsweep reported two of them as surviving, and it was right to.
The README also describes -tally, for planning and auditing a campaign swept in chunks, and -mutate boundary, which replaces a range comparison instead of deleting it; read them there.
data.excluded#A file the build excludes: A //go:build js && wasm file is not in a native build, so deleting a refusal in it changes nothing the command can see: the verdict would be SURVIVED when nothing looked. mutsweep reads GOOS and GOARCH as the go tool does. Naming an excluded file in -files or -only is an error (exit 2), and a directory sweep skips such files and names them.
data.hook#A sweep leaves a record, and -hook:
A sweep used to leave nothing but its report, which made this an analysis tool, not a gate: nothing failed when it was not run. That was measured, not argued. Over 2026-11-18/19 two sessions wrote “break-checked” over hand-made mutations while mutsweep sat installed, and when it was finally run it found three refusals no test held — all in code already merged.
So a delete-mode sweep files a record per file it swept completely, keyed by the SHA-256 of the file’s bytes, under the user config directory (MUTSWEEP_RECORDS overrides it). And:
mutsweep -hook # a Claude Code PreToolUse hook on Bash reads the hook payload and, when the command pushes with gitpush, refuses the push if it sends a non-test Go file holding refusals that:
the refusals in the file the push have no record at the bytes committed at HEAD refused: never swept as it is now have a record with SURVIVED or HUNG refused, naming the line were swept by an older walk that found fewer refusals refused have only caught by PANIC allowed, and said Editing a file changes its key, so a record cannot vouch for bytes it never saw — a comment included. The way out is the loop the report recommends: write the test a survivor asks for, re-ask that line alone with -only file.go:line, and the -only run updates the record for those bytes without re-sweeping the file.
⚠ caught by PANIC is not refused, deliberately. For an indexing guard — one whose deletion makes the next line index out of range — a panic is the only red any test can produce, so refusing it would make the gate impassable for correct code, and a gate that must always be waived teaches waiving.
⚠ What it does not see, said rather than implied: it judges HEAD, so a push of another checkout’s branch is judged by the wrong commit; it does not see ghmerge, which merges by number with no tree here to hash; a record is keyed by the guarded file only, so deleting the test that held a guard does not invalidate it; and it reads the command’s text, not a shell, so a push inside a quoted string or an eval is not seen.
When it cannot read — an unparseable payload, a repository with no origin/HEAD — it allows, and says so to the user through the hook’s systemMessage: an allowance that is not announced would be the gate-that-does-nothing again. The waiver is MUTSWEEP_SKIP=1 gitpush …, printed together with the files that went out unswept, because a waiver is made in public or not at all.
data.init#Init-clause refusals, and a deletio:
if v, err := f(); err != nil { return … } is a refusal like any other. It used to be skipped — not swept, not counted, not reported — so a sweep read as clean beside a guard whose test passed with the guard neutralised. Deleting such an if would delete the statement in its Init clause too, so it is mutated differently: the condition C becomes false && (C). The Init statement and every use of its variables stay, and the body is unreachable.
The same mutation is the fallback for an ordinary refusal whose deletion does not compile, because a variable used only in the condition is left unused. Before the fallback, “not a mutant” was often half of everything tried — 242 of 574 — and 8 of 11 refusals in one file read that way while being guards nothing tested. “Not a mutant” now means only that neither mutation compiles. -mutate boundary visits the conditions of init-clause ifs too.
