data.mutate#mutate:
Prove that a test can fail. Apply one exact source mutation, run the suite, restore whatever happens, and exit 0 only when the suite went red. Repository → Latest tag: v0.13.0 (git ls-remote --tags, 2026-11-22); this page is written from its README at v0.13.0, and the two are stated separately on purpose — which tag is current and which tag this page describes are different facts, and writing one where the other belongs is how a page comes to assert a version nobody checked it against. It has no dependency beyond the standard library.
$ mutate -file browse.go -name "mark repeats too" \ -from 'if !n.Repeat {' -to 'if true {' \ -- go test -run TestARepeatIsNot ./... mutate: mark repeats too — caught
data.mutsweep#mutsweep: the same question, of:
mutate proves one test can fail. mutsweep asks it of every refusal in a package: it deletes each one in turn, and says which ones nothing noticed.
$ mutsweep -dir structured -files blob.go,cell.go -run-in . -- go test ./... mutsweep: 38 refusals, 3m0s each at most, through "go test ./..." [1/38] caught blob.go:366 (size == 0) != (count == 0) 5s [15/38] SURVIVED blob.go:347 used <= 0 12s ... 38 refusals: 15 caught, 21 not mutants, 2 survived, 0 hung what nothing holds: SURVIVED blob.go:347 used <= 0 SURVIVED cell.go:98 !ok The README reports that over five runs on one project it put 574 guards through this and found thirteen that no test held.
data.only#Answering a report: -only:
After a sweep, tests are written for the survivors, and the question becomes whether they kill them, which is not the same as whether they pass. -only re-asks it for the named targets, spelled as the report prints them:
mutsweep -only map.go:163,map.go:628 -timeout 2m -- go test -count 1 ./... A target that matches no refusal is an error naming it, because an -only list goes stale and a sweep of nothing reads like a clean one.
data.panic#A panic is not an assertion:
“The suite went red” has two causes, and only one of them is a test. A test that asserts fails because it compared a value with the one it expected. A test that merely walks past a deleted guard fails because the line after it indexed past an array or dereferenced nil — a crash no author wrote an expectation for.
Twice in one day in go-numerics/special the only thing that made a mutated range guard red was such a panic (x < 512 written x <= 512 failing with index out of range, special#71, and x < jyFastMaxX the same way, special#73), and a sweep that counts any red as caught reported both as held. A panic red is luck: the next change that enlarges the table makes the mutant survive, silently. So a red suite is read once more, from go test -json events, and a panic-only red is given its own verdict and listed among the things nothing holds.
data.verdicts#Five verdicts, because two is n: verdict meaning caught the suite went red and a test printed an assertion line: the guard is held caught by PANIC the suite went red, the output holds a runtime panic and no test asserted: held by luck, and listed with the survivors SURVIVED the suite stayed green: nothing holds it not a mutant neither mutation compiled — the deletion, then false && (C) HUNG no answer in time: the guard is load-bearing and nothing says so The exit status is non-zero when anything survived, hung, or was caught only by a panic, so a sweep can stand as a CI gate. HUNG is not a theoretical category: deleting the check that a retry policy is honourable does not fail a suite, it makes the suite wait out an hour somebody mistyped into the wrong field.

data.branch-conflict#A @branch whose head is:
GitHub runs pull_request workflows against refs/pull/N/merge, which does not exist while the merge cannot be computed — so a conflicted pull request has no runs at all, by construction. prwait has refused CONFLICTING before counting checks since its first release, but the branch form supplied a fabricated mergeable: "MERGEABLE" — right for a bare branch, which has nothing to merge into, and a lie when the branch is a pull request’s head. The refusal was therefore unreachable from the form that avoids guessing a number, which is the form the fleet’s own rule prescribes (fixed in v0.11.0).
Measured 2026-11-18 on go-zpkg/zpkb#505: TIMEOUT after 30m0s — 0 checks, want at least 1, then three retriggers spent on a dropped-dispatch theory — Actions enabled, all workflows active, repository public, githubstatus operational — while gh pr view --json mergeable answered CONFLICTING in one call. The refusal now names the pull request, because a reader told “CONFLICTING” about a branch has no way to know which one said so.
⚠ The selection is by head, not by association: GitHub associates a commit with every pull request that contains it, so a branch cut from main is associated with whatever merged into main. Only a pull request whose headRefName is this branch says anything about what this branch would merge.
data.cost#What a poll costs, and why the defa:
-interval reads as how often to ask. It is really how much of a shared budget to spend, because a poll reads every target: prwait -repo O/R 78 79 80 82 costs exactly what four separate prwait processes cost. That is how the quota above reached zero — one session, four waits, each at a 45-second default that was written for one target (v0.14.0):
Target GraphQL REST a pull request or a @branch 1 — the check list (statusCheckRollup exists only in GitHub’s GraphQL schema) 1 — the head commit’s workflow runs (actions/runs?head_sha=) a !run 0 1, and no runs are read: a run target already is a run ⚠ The two budgets are separate and are never summed: 5000 REST calls an hour and 5000 GraphQL points, either of which can be spent while the other is untouched. The scaling below is set by the REST half, because that is the half that was measured at zero.
So the default is 45s per target, capped at 5m, which holds the hourly cost of a wait at roughly what one target costs instead of multiplying it:
The reason is printed to stderr before the first call is spent, because a default that silently differs from the documented 45 s is a tool lying quietly:
$ prwait -repo go-pkgx/pkgx 82 83 84 prwait: 3 targets, so the default interval is 2m15s rather than 45s — one poll spends one REST call per target (the head commit's workflow runs), and that budget is per USER, shared by every session here, Renovate included. -interval overrides this. … The cap is a deliberate choice of a human-usable interval over a constant budget: at 20 targets, linear growth would put 15 minutes between polls, so a verdict ready at minute 1 would arrive at minute 15 and the wait would read as a hang. Past the cap the cost is stated rather than held, with the figure it actually spends — a trade-off nobody is told about is one nobody can act on.
⛔ An explicit -interval is never scaled. A caller who names one has said what they want of the budget, and silently multiplying it would make the flag mean something other than what it reads — the same defect as the unscaled default, with the sign reversed.
data.install#Install: go install github.com/go-fleettools/prwait@latest It shells out to gh, which holds the authentication: prwait never reads, prints or passes a token.
data.named#The verdict names the commit it ju:
Every verdict carries the head it was decided at (@4f1c2ab above), because a wait that began on one commit and a head it ended with are different pieces of work. A target with no commit to name — a conflicted pull request has no head to judge — prints none rather than an empty @.
⛔ And a head that moves mid-wait is refused, not followed (v0.9.0). Naming the commit is necessary and not sufficient: a wait that silently re-points at a push the caller never asked about ends by printing a true statement about the wrong work.
$ prwait -repo go-tex/engine 752 go-tex/engine#752 MOVED @e87aa0a -> @2baff07 — the head changed while waiting; this wait judged neither, re-run against @2baff07 Neither commit was judged as a whole, so neither is reported as a verdict, and the exit status is 1. It holds for a branch (@main) and a run as much as for a pull request — a release gate waiting on the default branch must not answer about a commit that arrived after the one it was asked about, or the tag lands on something nobody judged. A SHA that one poll could not read is not a move: a blank answer is weather, and the retry loop already covers it.
data.per-user#A budget that is per user canno:
Since v0.15.0. Scaling one wait’s interval by its own targets is right and was not enough: the incident that emptied the quota was four processes, one per pull request, each pacing itself perfectly for the one target it knew about. The counter GitHub keeps is per user, so that is the granularity the pacing has to use.
A wait therefore records itself in /prwait/waits.json — per user by construction — and counts the targets the other live waits are already polling into its own interval:
$ prwait -repo go-x/y 82 prwait: 2 other wait(s) of this user are already polling 4 target(s) (pid 32374, started 4s ago, 3 target(s): go-x/y#78 go-x/y#79 go-x/y#80) (pid 32687, started 2s ago, 1 target(s): go-tex/engine#906) — the REST budget is per USER, shared with every session here and with Renovate, so one wait can take every target. prwait: pacing this wait for 5 target(s) in all (1 here, 4 elsewhere), so the interval is 3m45s rather than 45s. -interval overrides this. Four single-target waits now cost what one four-target wait costs. Measured on 2026-11-22, minutes after the release, the registry on one workstation held eight live waits from eight different sessions, each on a single pull request of a different repository — the incident’s own shape, now visible and paced.
It warns and paces; it does not refuse. With about twenty-five sessions sharing a machine, one thirty-minute wait that locked the others out of the only tool they are told to wait with would be switched off — by a flag, or by going back to gh pr checks --watch, which is the defect this tool exists to prevent.
And nothing about the bookkeeping can fail a wait. No cache directory, an unreadable file, a lock left behind by a killed wait: each is a line printed beside the verdict, never an exit status. An entry is dropped when its deadline has passed or when its process is gone — and “the process is gone” may only ever drop an entry the deadline would have kept, so a platform that cannot answer it says “cannot tell”, never “dead”. A wrong “false” there would quietly empty the registry and restore the per-process pacing; a wrong “true” only paces one wait conservatively until a deadline passes. A non-positive pid is a separate question — a malformed entry, not a dead process — so it is dropped on every platform, including those where liveness is unknowable.
data.prwait#prwait:
Wait until a pull request’s checks are finished, and refuse to call an empty check list a pass — or a complete, all-green one, when a workflow run for the same commit is red. data.quota#And a rate limit is not a verdict:
When GitHub refuses the call for the quota, nothing about the target was measured, so nothing is claimed about it (v0.13.0):
$ prwait -repo go-embedded-julia/julia 78 79 80 82 go-embedded-julia/julia#78 QUOTA — not a verdict: nothing about this target was measured. ⛔ the per-user REST quota is spent (0 of 5000 left). It resets at 20:45 CET, in 38m12s. The quota is per USER, not per token, so every session on this machine shares it — Renovate included. ⛔ 4 target(s) got no verdict at all: …#78, …#79, …#80, …#82 — the quota stopped the wait before they were read. Measured 2026-11-15: the account’s REST quota hit zero twice in one day, and both times this tool printed the raw gh: API rate limit exceeded … (HTTP 403) where its verdict goes, under exit 1 — the status of a red check. A caller reading only the status took “nothing could be measured” for “the pull request is red”, which is this tool’s own defect wearing its least recognisable face: an unread answer presenting itself as a negative one.
The retry made it worse. A failed query is weather here, so a quota was asked again three times at the poll interval — three more refusals, each spending a call against the very limit that was refusing. Weather has no reset time; a quota has one, advertised. So a quota now gets its own classification, its own hold, and its own exit status:
Held for, when the reset fits. The wait sleeps to the advertised reset and resumes. Costs nothing, and keeps the verdict. Refused early, when it does not. Spending the rest of the timeout to learn what /rate_limit already said is how four calls bought one fact. A secondary limit is reported as a secondary limit. /rate_limit cannot see it — “There is not a way to check the status of your secondary rate limit” — so when GitHub refuses for a rate limit while the instrument reports room, that is said in those words and marked as deduced. No reset is ever borrowed from the primary limit to stand in for one that does not exist. A measured red still outranks it. If anything was actually read as failing, the status stays 1. ⚠ GET /rate_limit is free of the primary limit only — “Calling this endpoint does not count against your primary rate limit, but it can count against your secondary rate limit” — so it is read once before the wait and once per refusal, never per poll.
data.rerun#A red that can no longer be re-run:
Past GitHub’s 30-day re-run window, gh run rerun answers 403 Unable to retry this workflow run because it was created over a month ago — so the red is permanent where it stands, and the only way to a fresh verdict is a ref you control (v0.12.0).
$ prwait -repo go-ansible/playbook 197 go-ansible/playbook#197 @c5dd86d FAIL test (macos-latest)=FAILURE ⛔ ci (pull_request run #412) was created 2026-10-12, 37 days ago: `gh run rerun` will answer 403 (GitHub allows a re-run for 30 days). This red cannot be refreshed where it stands. Reproduce the lane locally if it names your platform, or put the commit on a ref you control — `git cherry-pick` onto a branch in this repository — and let CI judge it there. That line exists because the question went unasked for ten days on that very pull request. It was handed back twice as “blocked: three routes tried, all closed” — and all three routes were ways to make that run go green, so they shared one premise and tested it once. Cherry-picked onto a branch in the target repository, the same commit came back 9/9 green, macos-latest included: the red belonged to the stale base, not to the change.
data.rule#The rule:
A pull request passes only when at least -min-checks checks exist, every one of them has finished, and every conclusion is acceptable. Absence is never evidence.
An obvious waiter asks “is anything still pending?” and stops when the answer is no; that waiter reported success on four pull requests that had never been built. A conflicted pull request gets no merge ref, so no workflow runs and its check list stays empty, and the same list is empty right after a push and for the life of a pull request whose workflow fails to parse. Also: a commit status is not a check run; CANCELLED is not a pass (NEUTRAL and SKIPPED are); UNKNOWN mergeability is not an answer; a timeout is a failure; an error from gh sinks the run.
data.runs#And a complete, all-green check lis:
A check run is created per job, so a workflow run that fails before its jobs are created leaves no check run at all: nothing red, nothing pending, nothing to count.
Measured on go-tex/go-tex.github.io#239, head 769bfee, 2026-11-09 — v0.5.0 printed PASS SUCCESS:3 and exited 0:
Asked Answered commits/769bfee/check-runs 3 check runs, all success, none pending actions/runs?head_sha=769bfee docs ✓, links ✓, pages failure, playground failure pages had created zero jobs and playground one of its three. Every property the check list can express was true, so from v0.6.0 the pull request and branch forms read the head commit’s workflow runs too and judge them by the same table — startup_failure, the conclusion only a run can carry, is a failure like any other.
Three refinements the same measurement forced:
The verdict is bound to the SHA, never to the branch name or the number: both move while a wait is running. An answer carrying no head commit is refused rather than judged on its checks alone. The SHA must be whole. head_sha=e18cc9b answers an empty list for a commit that has a run in progress; 40 characters finds it. An empty list is a legitimate state, so an abbreviation would pass as an absence. Refused before gh is reached. Only the latest run of each workflow, per event, is judged (v0.7.0). A commit carries the failed run and the retrigger that replaced it, and judging both leaves a commit that is now green unpassable forever. The event is part of that key because on that same commit a workflow_dispatch was green while the pull_request run was red — and that dispatch was started by hand to investigate the failure. A run started to look into a failure must not be able to clear it.
data.usage#Usage: prwait [-repo OWNER/REPO] [flags] ... Target Asks 82 or OWNER/REPO#82 a pull request: may this land @main or OWNER/REPO@main a branch: is what landed green !40237685388 or OWNER/REPO!402... a workflow run: did that dispatch finish, and how Flag Default -repo repository for bare numbers -interval 45s × every target this user is waiting on, capped at 5m how often to ask — see the cost of a poll and per user, not per process; given explicitly, it is used as typed and never scaled -timeout 30m give up after this, per run -min-checks 1 how many checks must exist before a pass is possible -gh gh the gh binary to ask -min-checks 0 is refused, because it would restore the defect this tool exists for. The number is one for the whole run, so split the run when suites differ.

data.install#Install and usage: go install github.com/go-fleettools/staletools@latest staletools [-all] [-want go1.27.1] [dir...] With no directory it looks at $GOBIN (or $GOPATH/bin, or ~/go/bin) and ~/.local/bin. -want compares against another toolchain: “what would be stale if we moved to this?”. It has no dependency beyond the standard library.
data.releases#-releases: staletools -releases The default axis asks what a tool was built with; this one asks what it is: which installed tools are an older release of themselves. A marker → flags those in a directory the shell searches, ahead of those in one nothing reads. The oracle is go list -m -versions, not a tag listing, and a tool built from an unreleased commit is reported under its own heading rather than mislabelled as behind.
data.staletools#staletools:
Which installed Go tools were built with an older toolchain, and, of those, which actually parse Go source, because only for those is staleness a wrong answer rather than an old binary. $ staletools READ GO SOURCE and are behind go1.27.1 — these do not fail, they MISREPORT: gopls go1.26.4 ~/go/bin go install golang.org/x/tools/gopls@latest ... INSTALLED TWICE with different toolchains — PATH order decides which runs: agentsync go1.27.1 ~/.local/bin go1.26.4 ~/go/bin 81 Go tool(s), 29 behind go1.27.1, 8 of those read Go source (An excerpt of the README’s example, measured on its author’s machine.)
Exit 0 no source-reading tool is behind, and nothing is shadowed 1 something is behind or shadowed 2 refused: a directory that cannot be read
data.why#Why the distinction: A CLI built with go1.26 runs under a go1.27 toolchain: it is old, not broken. But a tool that analyses Go source embeds go/types and go/parser from its build toolchain, and built with go1.26 it cannot read go1.27: it emits type errors about the standard library and then reports on whatever it managed to load, so the output reads like findings. staletools finds those tools from the dependency list of the binary (golang.org/x/tools, honnef.co/go/tools and the like), not from a list of names. It also reports a tool installed in two directories with different toolchains. The totals are always printed, zeros included.

data.lead#A lead, not a verdict:
Both shapes are correct over input the program produced itself, so every hit has to be read by somebody who knows where the bytes come from. What the tool owes in return: it parses rather than greps; it names what it could not read; it prints both denominators (“66 repositories read, 0 NOT read”); and reading nothing is a failure, exiting non-zero.
A directory is scanned in place so that the instrument can be checked against a checkout of a version that had the defect: it must find it, and find nothing on the fixed version.
data.limits#What it does not cover: The image decoders are a written-out list, so a third-party HEIC or JPEG 2000 reader is a decoder it does not know. A ZIP entry read through a helper in another file is missed: the two shapes are judged within one file. It holds 100 % statement coverage, gated in CI.
data.unbounded#unbounded:
Which repositories read a ZIP entry, or decode an image, without a ceiling? Repository → Latest tag: v0.3.0 (git ls-remote --tags, 2026-11-15); this page is written from its README at v0.2.0, and the two are stated separately on purpose: which tag is current and which tag this page describes are different facts. The README at the tag this page describes gives no install line; one was added on main on 2026-10-26, after checking that it builds (the command is in cmd/unbounded, the module root is not a main package):
go install github.com/go-fleettools/unbounded/cmd/unbounded@latest unbounded go-odf go-pdfkit go-gfx # organisations: listed, cloned, parsed unbounded ./some/checkout # a directory is scanned in place go-gfx/gfx svg/svg.go:817 image.Decode and nothing in this file asks DecodeConfig first go-pdfkit/pdfkit image.go:99 png.Decode and nothing in this file asks DecodeConfig first 66 repositories read, 0 NOT read 2 open a ZIP, 15 decode an image, 4 lead(s) to look at (The README’s example output.)
data.why#Why: Both shapes are how a few hundred bytes of input become a few gigabytes of memory: io.ReadAll on a ZIP entry (an .ods of 67,206 bytes inflated to 64 MiB and held 222.9 MiB), and image.Decode before image.DecodeConfig (a 75-byte PNG claiming 10000 x 10000 allocated 381.6 MiB). A fix does not travel: a sibling repository carried the identical defect for weeks because nobody looked, and this is the sweep that follows a fix across its siblings.
